patterns.label: Standard Form
patterns.explain: Standard form of the article: הַ with a dagesh forte in the first consonant of the noun, which doubles it.

patterns.label: Compensatory Lengthening
patterns.explain: The noun begins with a guttural that rejects the dagesh (א, ר, or sometimes ע). The article’s short vowel lengthens within its own vowel class: pataḥ becomes qameṣ, so הַ becomes הָ. This is compensatory lengthening.

patterns.label: Implicit Doubling
patterns.explain: The noun begins with ה, ח, or sometimes ע. The guttural rejects the dagesh, but the article’s vowel does not change: it stays הַ (pataḥ), and the guttural is understood to be doubled by implication. This is implicit doubling.

patterns.label: Exceptional Forms: הָ before an accented הָ
patterns.explain: Exceptional form (singular, e.g. הָהָרָה, “to the mountain”). Normally a ה lets the article stay short (הַ). But when that ה has a qameṣ and is accented, the implicit doubling can no longer be pronounced, and the article’s pataḥ lengthens to qameṣ to compensate: הַ becomes הָ. This is compensatory lengthening.

patterns.label: Exceptional Forms: הֶ before an unaccented הָ or עָ
patterns.explain: Exceptional form (plural, e.g. הֶהָרִים, “the mountains”). Hebrew avoids two “a” sounds in a row when the second one is unaccented. When the ה or ע has a qameṣ but no accent, the article’s pataḥ changes to segol: הַ becomes הֶ. This is vowel dissimilation.

patterns.label: SQNMLVY: vocal sheva
patterns.explain: SQNMLVY exception: a sibilant or one of י ו ל מ נ ק that has a vocal sheva may lose the dagesh forte, so the article is הַ with no doubling written.

patterns.label: SQNMLVY: extended environment
patterns.explain: SQNMLVY exception, extended environment: a SQNMLVY consonant with a short vowel, standing before another doubled consonant, may lose the dagesh forte after the article.

patterns.label: Pausal Lengthening
patterns.explain: In a pausal form (at the end of a verse or major clause, or before a strong disjunctive accent) a short vowel often lengthens within its own vowel class, the same change as compensatory lengthening: pataḥ becomes qameṣ. Here the article’s pataḥ has lengthened to qameṣ (הָ) in a pausal form, even though no guttural forced it.

passages.title: Genesis 1:1–5
passages.note: The opening of the Bible: standard הַ + dagesh forte, compensatory lengthening before א and implicit doubling before ח.

passages.title: Genesis 8:5–7
passages.note: Five patterns in one short passage, including הֶ before ה.

passages.title: Genesis 15:19–21
passages.note: A list of peoples, including the SQNMLVY exception: הַיְבוּסִי.

Gen.40.3.n: In this digital text the dagesh in the ט is not written, but the word is standard form: הַ + a dagesh forte in the first letter of the noun.
